The baseline is the library's own pure-Go table-lookup path, not Intel ISA-L or a C library, and the README has no ISA-L comparison. PR #336 (2026-04-21) refreshed the Performance, Leopard and Reconstruct tables together, so the tables come from one update and not mixed releases. The README carries a patent warning about erasure-coding lawsuits and offers a -tags=nopshufb build that removes the PSHUFB paths.

corrections.caveats: This is multi-buffer throughput: 8 (AVX2) or 16 (AVX512) independent hashes per core. The README says it does not speed up a single MD5 sum, and that one hash on a server runs at about half the throughput, so it helps only servers hashing many large streams at once. When these numbers were taken, the crypto/md5 baseline on amd64 was hand-written scalar assembly (Marc Bevand's md5block_amd64.s, present in Go's release-branch.go1.21 tree), not compiler output. Current Go master has md5 assembly only for riscv64 and s390x. The README's benchmark names (BenchmarkParallel/32KB-4, built with benchcmp from crypto-md5.txt and avx512.txt) do not match the current test functions (BenchmarkCryptoMd5Parallel, BenchmarkAvx2Parallel, BenchmarkAvx512Parallel), so the exact harness revision is not identified. The Go version is unstated. The block benchmark times the raw 64-byte block function on 16 lanes, without padding or finalization, against a full crypto/md5 Write+Sum. Commit #32 (2022) added an option to disable AVX512 on CPUs that throttle. The AVX2 kernel is taken essentially unchanged from igneous-systems/md5vec.

notes: Numbers match the README, and an AVX2 table (up to 4.09x) is also given; the record wrongly said only the AVX512 table has numbers. Shortcomings to record: Go version unstated; the baseline crypto/md5 was scalar assembly at the time, not compiler output; the gain is multi-buffer only (no single-hash speedup); the README harness names differ from the current tests; the repo is stale (last commit 2025-04-02, 216 stars). The license is Apache-2.0 plus BSD-3-Clause for the Go-derived files; both are OSI-approved, so it stays copyable.

reject_reason: other: wrong-answer fast path. The timed NASM and hybrid AVX kernels do not compute the 512x512 matrix product: M2 rows are read at the wrong offsets, the horizontal sum drops the upper 128-bit lane, the pure-NASM driver never stores a result, and the hybrid C kernel uses overlapping 32-byte loads at 16-byte offsets. The README table is also internally inconsistent.
tier_reason: The README table does compare scalar C/C++ with the NASM XMM/YMM and hybrid kernels on a named CPU (Ryzen 5 5600X) with stated gcc flags. However, the timed kernels produce wrong results, there is no correctness check, and the table contradicts itself, so the numbers carry no usable evidence. If the entry is kept, list it as D.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table, 512x512 single-precision matmul on a Ryzen 5 5600X: scalar C ~0.6 s (<1 GFLOP/s), scalar C++ ~1.3 s, NASM XMM ~0.29 s (stated ~10 GFLOP/s), NASM YMM ~0.0098 s (~28 GFLOP/s), hybrid C/C++ + ASM ~0.010 to 0.020 s. YMM is about 61x faster than scalar C (derived from page data). The XMM row is inconsistent: 2x512^3 FLOP in 0.29 s is about 0.93 GFLOP/s, not ~10 (derived from page data). The README text claims SSE gives 5-9x over C, but the table shows about 2.1x. It also claims about 30x for AVX-512, but there is no zmm code and the 5600X has no AVX-512.
corrections.baseline: naive scalar triple loop computing A*B^T: C version uses float with float** row arrays (PureC/Mmulti.c, timed with clock() including result-row mallocs); C++ version uses double in vector<vector<double>> passed by value (PureC++/Mmulti.cpp)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: README states gcc -O3 -mavx -msse -mfma; the kernels are NASM (simdcompileymm.sh, simdcompilexmm.sh: nasm -f elf64, gcc -c with no optimisation flags for matrix_generator.c); there is no build script for the PureC/PureC++ baselines, only checked-in binaries
corrections.caveats: Wrong-answer kernels. (1) SIMDMProduct.asm adds 32 bytes to r15 after each dot_product_ymm call, but the kernel has already advanced r15 by 1920 bytes, so successive M2 'rows' start 1952 bytes apart instead of 2048. (2) The driver discards the xmm0 result, so no output matrix is ever written. (3) The final vhaddps pair plus a low-lane read sums only the lower 128-bit lane, dropping half the partial sums. (4) HybridC/Ymm/SIMDMMultyhybrid.c loads 32-byte ymm registers at byte offsets 0, 16, 32 and 48, so the loads overlap and only 20 of every 32 floats are read; it also relies on ymm state persisting across separate asm() statements. There is no correctness test. The timed FLOP count does equal a 512^3 multiply-add, so the time reflects real vector work, but not a matrix product. The table is internally inconsistent: the XMM row is 0.29 s but ~10 GFLOP/s, and the text says SSE gives 5-9x and AVX-512 gives ~30x with no zmm code. The XMM kernel uses four accumulators, not the stated 2x unroll. The kernels use vmulps+vaddps, not FMA. The C++ baseline is double precision, with matrices copied by value. The scalar baselines keep a strict-FP single-accumulator reduction that gcc cannot vectorize without -ffast-math, and they have no build script. The asm timer divides RDTSC by a hard-coded 3.69305 GHz.

notes: Reject per the stb-zip and fast_resize precedents (the fast path computes a different result): every timed asm path miscomputes the product (wrong M2 stride, lane-dropping horizontal add, results never stored, overlapping hybrid loads), and the README table contradicts itself (XMM 0.29 s labelled ~10 GFLOP/s; an AVX-512 claim with no zmm code on a Zen 3 CPU).
